note: Parse only. What a client DOES with a limit view - pre-spend admission, backoff, shedding its own traffic - is the `admission` list; this list fixes what the view IS, so the three SDKs cannot each invent a different reading of the same response. Bodies are the real IngestResponse / ApiError shapes from crates/api. Signals arrive two ways: as body fields on POST /v1/events, and as X-LightTrack-* headers on every ingest door (the batch door answers multi-status and the OTLP door answers in the exporter's envelope, so neither has a body field to put them in). The body wins where both are present.

limits.name: accepted-with-proximity
limits.why: An accepted write carries the worst usage ratio among the rules that applied, so a client can see the wall coming without polling /v1/limits/status.

limits.name: accepted-under-graduated-shedding
limits.why: shed_fraction rising is the signal to slow down BEFORE the hard 429s start. It is omitted entirely when nothing is throttling, so absent and 0.0 must not be conflated.

limits.name: accepted-no-limits-configured
limits.why: A project with no limits reports no ratio at all. null means unknown, not zero - a client that read it as 0.0 would think it had infinite headroom.

limits.name: accepted-duplicate-replay
limits.why: A retried POST of an already-recorded event returns the original outcome. Still accepted; nothing is double-counted.

limits.name: hard-cap-429
limits.why: A hard cap advertises the wait until its window ages out. Header name casing is not guaranteed by HTTP, so the lookup has to be case-insensitive - this case spells it Retry-After.

error.message: project 'demo' is over its monthly cost cap

limits.name: graduated-shed-429
limits.why: A shed asks for a short pause, not the window. Same status, different schedule - and this case spells the header lower-case.

error.message: shedding: 40% of ingest is being refused

limits.name: rejected-bad-request
limits.why: Not every rejection is a limit. A 400 must not be read as back-pressure, or a client would sleep an hour over a typo.

limits.name: overloaded-503
limits.why: Back-pressure from the server rather than from a project's budget. It carries a Retry-After too, and a client should honour it, but it is not rate_limited.

limits.name: unparseable-retry-after
limits.why: Retry-After may legally be an HTTP-date. The SDKs do not parse dates; the contract is that an unreadable value is null, never 0 (which would mean retry immediately).

limits.name: error-without-a-body
limits.why: A proxy can return a bare status. Everything unknown stays null.

limits.name: proximity-from-headers-when-the-body-has-no-room
limits.why: The batch door answers multi-status: the project's position is not a property of item 7, so it cannot be a body field. The OTLP door answers in the exporter's own envelope. Both carry the signal in headers instead, and a client that only read the body was blind on two of the three ingest doors.

limits.name: body-wins-over-headers
limits.why: On POST /v1/events both channels carry the same admission, so they cannot disagree - but the precedence has to be stated rather than left to whichever the implementation happened to read first, or a proxy that rewrites a header would silently change a client's verdict.

limits.name: binding-scope-names-what-is-actually-full
limits.why: 0.94 alone tells a client to stop everything. 0.94 on model=gpt-4o tells it to route the next call elsewhere and keep working. binding_rule is the other half: the server's shed decision is a hash of (rule_id, event_id), so without the rule's identity a client can run the same function and never reach the same answer.

limits.name: retry-after-stripped-by-a-proxy
limits.why: Retry-After does not always survive the trip: proxies drop it and browser fetch stacks hide it. X-LightTrack-Retry-After mirrors it so the back-off schedule arrives anyway. It is only a fallback - where both are present the standard header is the one that counts.

limits.name: a-mirrored-header-never-overrides-the-standard-one
limits.why: If the two ever disagree, the RFC-defined header is the contract and the mirror is the copy.
